extracted.intended_audience: general public, householders and caregivers responsible for cleaning or disinfecting sick rooms and preventing spread of infectious disease
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, household-level guidance for disinfecting rooms, clothing, and utensils and for preventing spread of tuberculosis and pneumonia (how to choose agents, concentrations, procedures, and precautions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and aim of disinfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinfection is a determined effort to destroy the carriers of disease while temporarily absent from the human body; to kill germs after they leave a sick person so they cannot infect others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus disinfection on the location where the patient was confined (air, walls, floors, contents). Recognize limits: germs are invisible and location uncertain; cannot disinfect everything, so concentrate on likely contaminated surroundings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of disinfecting agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinfecting agents are divided into two groups: heat (various forms) and chemicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose heat (steam, boiling, dry heat) where possible for its superior penetrating and destructive power; use chemicals where heat is impractical (on the body or delicate objects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish disinfectants, antiseptics, deodorizers
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinfectants: destroy bacteria; antiseptics: interfere with or retard growth without destroying bacteria and are milder for tissues; deodorizers: mask smells without disinfecting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use antiseptics (not strong disinfectants) on wounds to avoid tissue damage. Do not rely on deodorizers as disinfectants; avoid accepting products that are merely scented as if they disinfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward patented disinfectants
rubrics_metrics.description: Patented or fancy-named preparations usually add little over basic chemicals; the active poisons are the same inexpensive raw materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer basic, proven chemicals (lime, carbolic acid, etc.) bought cheaply; do not overpay for branding when the basic chemical is equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportioning disinfectant volume to material
rubrics_metrics.description: A disinfecting solution must be reasonably proportioned in volume to the amount of material to be disinfected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid under-dosing (e.g., using a single pail of hot water for many linens) or token actions (burning a tablespoon of sulfur in an open room). Ensure adequate quantity and contact to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of disinfecting gases for rooms and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Two gases are recommended for disinfecting rooms after infectious patients: sulfurous acid (from burned sulfur) and formaldehyde gas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one of these in every case after an infectious patient; consider contents (blankets, curtains) which gases penetrate poorly unless moistened or sent to steam sterilizer. Treat movable contents separately when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sulfur fumigation procedure and dosage
rubrics_metrics.description: When sulfur is burned it produces sulfurous acid gas; proper amount is 3 pounds per 1000 cubic feet of air space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make room absolutely air-tight by pasting cracks around windows, sashes, doors, and baseboards. Moisten textiles to increase penetration. Burn sulfur in a pan placed on bricks inside a tub of water; moisten sulfur with alcohol for ignition. Keep room closed at least 24 hours. After fumigation, air and then wipe woodwork with carbolic solution as additional safeguard. Beware of fire risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formaldehyde fumigation procedure and dosage
rubrics_metrics.description: Formaldehyde gas is generated from solidified formaldehyde (formalin) heated; use about 20 ounces of formalin per 1000 cubic feet of space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seal room carefully as for sulfur. Place generator in water or sand to avoid fire hazard. Keep room closed at least 12 hours, then thoroughly air. Penetration is limited; send mattresses and bulky items to steam sterilizer. Remove odor with ammonia if room is to be used soon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liquid disinfectants general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain liquids (carbolic acid, coal-tar products, bichloride of mercury, chloride of lime, etc.) are proven to kill bacteria on contact and are convenient and inexpensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select liquids that do not overly damage fabrics/metals and use at recommended concentrations; many bottled combinations add little value beyond basic chemicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbolic acid (phenol) concentrations and uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Carbolic acid: 2% solution for wiping woodwork, furniture, floors; 5% solution for destroying organic matter with heavy germ load (receiving sputum, vomiting material, fecal matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 5% is practically saturated and should never be used on living human tissue. Carbolic acid does not disinfect air and is ineffective as a room deodorizer. Label and keep away from children; do not pour it around as a token measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coal-tar products (cresols/creosols) strength and advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Coal-tar products in about a 4% solution will destroy bacteria in a few hours and have roughly three times the power of carbolic acid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are less interfered with by albuminous material (e.g., sputum) than carbolic acid, so are preferred when organic material is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrosive sublimate (bichloride of mercury) usage and precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Bichloride of mercury is very active; use about 1 part to 3000 parts water (1 ounce to 25 gallons) for general scrubbing of woodwork, floors, walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store and mix in brassware or earthenware; avoid tin or iron. Albuminous material reduces effectiveness but can be counteracted by adding salt (~4 tsp per gallon). Very poisonous—keep away from children; consider adding coloring to solution to prevent accidental ingestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chloride of lime (bleaching powder) concentration and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Chloride of lime is effective in a 1% solution (1 lb per ~12 gallons of water); the active agent is the chloride and it must be well stirred into organic matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saucers placed around a room are ineffective against air/ floor germs. It erodes clothes and is unsuitable for disinfecting towels. Dry powder sprinkled is generally ineffective unless later dissolved and washed into drains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milk of lime (slaked lime) preparation and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Milk of lime is made by slaking building lime to a fine powder and mixing with water; used as a whitewash and general disinfectant for walls, cellars, drains and privies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must come into intimate contact with contaminated matter; useful poured into drains and used liberally where bacteria may thrive; avoid relying on dry powder sprinkled around.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soap and hot water as antiseptic practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary soap plus hot water is an excellent antiseptic, especially combined with washing soda for boiling clothes; soap and hot water remove germs from hands and utensils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wash soiled hands before eating; wash dishes from sick room separately and in boiling water with soap/soda. Ammonia is less effective than washing soda for laundering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinfection by heat principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat (steam, boiling water, dry heat) is the most effective and penetrating method to destroy bacteria when sufficient temperature is maintained for sufficient time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fire only when acceptable to destroy contaminated material. Prefer moist heat (boiling/steam) for liquids and fabrics; dry heat for glassware/metal only when appropriate temperatures can be achieved without damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dry heat parameters and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Dry heat (e.g., oven) must reach about 150°C (300°F) and be maintained for at least an hour to disinfect glassware/earthenware/metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dry heat is unsuitable for many household items and cannot penetrate bulky textiles; kitchen ovens are not generally recommended for household disinfection tasks requiring penetration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiling water parameters and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Boiling water will absolutely kill disease-bearing bacteria if objects are actually boiled for five minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Water must be boiling during exposure (not merely once boiled earlier). Adding a tablespoonful of washing soda per gallon improves efficacy. Wash dishes used by sick persons separately in boiling water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steam sterilization usage and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Steam is often preferable to hot water for delicate fabrics (cotton, wool) and should be applied 30–60 minutes depending on item size; pressurized steam is required to penetrate large, dense bundles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small garments can be steamed at home (steamer for puddings); mattresses, pillows, and bulky furniture should be sent to a professional steam sterilizer; ordinary household methods may not reach centers of tightly rolled bundles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural agents: drying, sunlight, soil — utility and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Drying kills many germs over long periods; direct sunlight can kill many bacteria in hours; soil harbors competing harmless germs that reduce virulence of disease germs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These natural methods help but are unreliable and slow—do not depend on them alone. Sunlight and ventilation are beneficial for prevention (e.g., sunny rooms). Burial of wastes in soil can reduce viability but should not replace chemical/heat disinfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tuberculosis primary prevention: control of sputum ('Don't spit')
rubrics_metrics.description: Tuberculosis is mainly spread by sputum that dries into dust and becomes airborne; main prevention is faithful care of expectorations—'Don't spit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spit on sidewalks, floors, shops; use gutters or spittoons. Keep personal spittoons half full of water and clean daily with hot water. Cough into handkerchief or cover mouth. Promote fresh air in living and working spaces (keep bedroom windows open day and night). Wash hands before eating and do not neglect colds or coughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual resistance and environmental reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals with higher vitality and more exposure to fresh air (outdoors, vigorous) resist tuberculosis more than those confined indoors and fatigued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevention includes building and maintaining general health and sanitary living conditions as well as direct disinfection measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumptive patient precautions for expectorations
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients with consumption must treat sputum as 'poison' and ensure every particle is disinfected or destroyed immediately after expectoration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expectorate into vessels filled with carbolic acid solution or into water which will afterwards be boiled. Ensure prompt, consistent disposal and disinfection to prevent household transmission (including items like blankets removed before fumigation).
